standard.title: European Imperial Expansion and Movement of Peoples
standard.description: the causes and effects of European imperial expansion and the movement of peoples in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, and the different responses to colonisation and migration
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied pre-modern and early modern societies including Medieval Europe, ancient empires, and Asia-Pacific societies in Year 8. They understand how power, authority, and cultural interaction shaped historical societies, and have worked with the concepts of turning points, continuity and change, and significant individuals. They have not yet studied the modern period (late 18th century onward) or the specific mechanisms of European imperial expansion, forced migration, or the causes of population movements in the industrial age.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify and describe the causes and effects of European imperial expansion and population movement in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, and explain different responses to colonisation and migration.

nodes.label: Push and pull factors of population movement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe a range of push factors (e.g. Agricultural Revolution, Industrial Revolution, famine, persecution, forced migration) and pull factors (e.g. employment, land, freedom) driving population movement in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and describe at least one push factor and one pull factor from the period using a concrete historical example.
nodes.typical_width: Describe a range of push and pull factors across multiple population groups — including voluntary migration, forced migration (slavery, convict transportation), and flight from famine or persecution — drawing on the elaboration examples.
wider: Examine how push and pull factors operated differently for different social groups (e.g. enslaved Africans had no pull factor — their movement was entirely coerced) to complicate a simple push-pull model

Investigate how the Agricultural Revolution in Britain created both push factors (rural unemployment from enclosures) and was itself a consequence of earlier population and economic shifts — examining the relationship between causes
Compare the push and pull factors for two distinct migration streams (e.g. Irish famine emigration vs convict transportation) to assess how agency and coercion varied
nodes.hinge_reason: The push-pull framework is the conceptual scaffold for the entire descriptor. If students conflate push and pull, or fail to distinguish voluntary from forced migration, their understanding of effects and responses (Nodes 2–4) will be structurally weak — they will not be able to analyse why different groups responded differently to colonisation.

response_modes.reason: Invest in explicit modelling of the push-pull distinction with concrete examples before students apply it independently. Common error: treating all migration as voluntary choice.
Widening to multiple migration streams (Irish famine, slavery, convict transportation) prevents students from anchoring the framework to a single case type.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The push-pull framework is pedagogically rich because different population groups represent a spectrum from full agency (free settlers) to complete coercion (enslaved peoples) — this spectrum is a powerful analytical tool for discussing power, choice, and historical conditions.
success_criteria: Identifies and describes at least two distinct push factors and two distinct pull factors, drawn from different population groups or migration events
Distinguishes between voluntary migration and forced migration with at least one example of each

nodes.label: Effects of colonisation on colonised peoples
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the effects of European imperial expansion on colonised peoples, including dispossession, disease, and destruction of traditional society and culture.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two distinct effects of colonisation on colonised peoples, with reference to a specific historical context.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the effects of colonisation across dispossession, disease, and cultural destruction in a specific colonial context; explain how these effects were interconnected and often compounding.
wider: Examine the effects of colonisation on First Nations Australians specifically — including frontier conflict, dispossession, the spread of European disease, destruction of cultural practices, and the Stolen Generations — to ground the abstract effects in a well-documented case

Compare the effects of colonisation across two different colonised societies (e.g. Indigenous Australians vs enslaved Africans in the Americas) to examine how the nature of colonisation shaped its effects

Investigate the long-term demographic effects of colonisation — population collapse in First Nations communities, the trans-Atlantic slave trade's demographic impact on West Africa — using historical data
nodes.hinge_reason: Students need a substantive understanding of colonial effects before they can meaningfully engage with responses to colonisation (Node 4). Without this, responses to colonisation appear motivationless — students will not understand why colonised peoples resisted, adapted, or were devastated.

response_modes.reason: Use multiple colonial contexts (Australian, American, African) to prevent students from treating one case as typical of all colonisation.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The effects of colonisation are pedagogically rich because they are still contested and live — connecting historical effects to present-day outcomes (e.g. Stolen Generations, intergenerational trauma) provides meaningful contemporary relevance.
success_criteria: Identifies and describes at least three distinct effects of colonisation (e.g. dispossession, disease, cultural destruction) with reference to a specific historical context
Explains how at least two of these effects were connected or compounding rather than isolated

nodes.label: Scale and geography of population movement — using data
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine and interpret historical data on the movement of peoples, including the scale, geographic spread, and nations involved in population movements of the period.
nodes.minimum_width: Use one data source (e.g. map, table, or statistics) to describe the scale or geographic spread of one population movement of the period.
nodes.typical_width: Examine data on the movement of peoples — including the transatlantic slave trade (numbers transported, nations involved) and Irish famine emigration (numbers, destinations) — to describe patterns of movement, scale, and geographic reach.
wider: Compare data sets across two different population movements (e.g. slave trade vs convict transportation vs Irish emigration) to analyse differences in scale, direction, and the nations involved
Investigate how historians have constructed and contested data on the transatlantic slave trade, and assess what the data does and does not reveal about individual lives
Use maps and statistical sources together to explain both the scale and the geographic logic of population movement — examining why people moved from specific origins to specific destinations

response_modes.reason: Using data across multiple movement types (slave trade, Irish famine, convict transportation) grounds abstract numbers in distinct human experiences and prevents false equivalence between voluntary and forced movements.

success_criteria: Uses at least one data source to describe the scale or geographic spread of a population movement
Identifies the nations of origin and destination involved in at least one movement stream

nodes.label: Different responses to colonisation and migration
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain different responses to colonisation and migration, including resistance, accommodation, adaptation, and the ways colonised peoples maintained or asserted their identity and agency.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two different responses to colonisation or migration, identifying who responded and in what context.
nodes.typical_width: Explain different responses to colonisation and migration across at least two population groups — including examples of resistance, accommodation, cultural adaptation, and economic contribution; explain why responses differed based on the context and conditions of each group.
wider: Examine how First Nations Australians responded to colonisation through a range of strategies — frontier resistance, economic contribution to colonial industries, adoption of Christian practices — and assess how these responses are represented in historical sources
Investigate the responses of Irish emigrants to their new host societies (USA, Canada, Australia) and analyse how responses varied by destination and circumstance

Examine how enslaved peoples in the Americas resisted enslavement — through everyday resistance, cultural preservation, and organised rebellion — and assess how these responses challenged the colonial system

response_modes.reason: Widening to multiple response types and population groups is essential to avoid a passive or victimhood-only framing of colonised peoples — responses must include agency, resistance, and adaptation.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: This node is where students can actively engage with historical agency — examining how colonised and displaced peoples were not simply victims but actors who responded, resisted, and adapted. This is pedagogically significant and connects to contemporary historical debates.
success_criteria: Identifies and explains at least two different responses to colonisation or migration, specifying who responded and why
Explains how context (e.g. degree of coercion, available options, cultural resources) shaped the nature of the response
